title: Twins are coming. Should we stretch for a RM1 million family house?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #203 | WORK LIKE DOG FOR A LANDED HOME. WORTH IT?
excerpt: A 30-year-old banker with twins on the way wants a RM1 million Kota Damansara house shared with his brother. Sean suggests renting on and buying an apartment one income can carry first.

qa.asker: J, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: J is 30 and earns about RM7,000 a month; his fiancée's commission income ranges from RM4,000 to RM12,000, and they are expecting twins. They rent a single-storey house in PJ for RM1,300 and have about RM100,000 in savings. He wants a RM1 million leasehold double-storey house in Kota Damansara as a family home for his father and siblings too, which would take about RM200,000 up front with touch-ups and RM4,000 a month, shared with his brother.
qa.question: Should he commit to the house and work hard to pay for it, or keep renting until his early 40s?
qa.quote: You don't actually need it now, it's only for romantic reasons.
qa.answer: Keep renting for now, and buy a home on his own that fits one person's budget, around RM500,000 to RM600,000, ideally a subsale with a three-bedroom layout. Live there for five to eight years, then upgrade to a bigger family home once the twins start school.

reasons.title: Newborns strain both money and time
reasons.body: With savings used up and RM4,000 a month to pay, every sick day and every difficult boss becomes a crisis. Babies may also mean daycare costs, and they don't need a landed house, only space for their carers.

reasons.title: Shared names need a clear exit
reasons.body: If his brother puts in money, agree his share and the price at which J would buy him out later. A leasehold house can lose value nearer 60 years left, though leases in Selangor have often been extended.

reasons.title: If he buys, keep the savings
reasons.body: If the seller agrees to a higher selling price, the bank may lend more for renovation and costs. Keep the savings in a flexi loan account as an emergency fund.

reasons.title: A landed home costs more than the instalment
reasons.body: Roofs, plumbing, gates and air conditioners all need fixing. A three-bedroom apartment can house his father and sister just as well, and is far easier to run.

actions: Stay in the current rental through the birth and the first year.
Shortlist PJ apartments or homes within one income's budget, ideally where rent covers 85% to 90% of the instalment.
Work out the new monthly budget, including childcare, before committing to anything.
If buying with his brother, put the ownership split and buy-out terms in writing first.
Plan to upgrade to a family home once the twins reach primary school.
qa.caveat: If they are comfortable with the stress and the bank approves a larger loan that preserves their savings, buying the landed house is workable. Sean admits he has seen many big family homes left empty, so his view reflects his own experience.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #203. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in February 2023.
